title: Integrated Rate Laws and Half-Life (Zero, First, Second Order)

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Chemical Kinetics

expression: Zero order: [A] = [A]₀ − kt, T½ = [A]₀/2k  ;  First order: k = (1/t)ln([A]₀/[A]), T½ = 0.693/k
explanation: Each reaction order has a distinct integrated rate law and half-life dependence. For a ZERO order reaction, concentration decreases linearly with time, and half-life is DIRECTLY proportional to initial concentration. For a FIRST order reaction, half-life is a CONSTANT, completely independent of initial concentration — this distinctive independence is the most reliable experimental signature used to identify a first-order process (like radioactive decay).

variables.meaning: Concentration at time t, and initial concentration

variables.unit: depends on order (e.g. s⁻¹ for first order)

workedExample.scenario: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0231 s⁻¹.
workedExample.result: T½ ≈ 30 s (same regardless of starting concentration)

commonMistakes: Assuming half-life is always constant regardless of order — this special independence from initial concentration is a UNIQUE signature of first-order kinetics only, not zero- or second-order.
Mixing up which order gives a straight-line plot with which variable — zero order gives a straight line for [A] vs t; first order for ln[A] vs t; second order for 1/[A] vs t.
genZNote: First-order half-life doesn't care how much you started with — same clock, every single time.
